segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents; rather, it was so that the works of God might be displayed in him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: We must work the works of the one who sent me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, and smeared the mud on the man’s eyes,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (which means Sent). So he went and washed, and came back seeing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the neighbors and those who had seen him before, when he was a beggar, began saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Others said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “No, but he looks like him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man himself kept saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am the one.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How were your eyes opened?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The man called Jesus made mud and smeared it on my eyes and told me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed, and I gained my sight.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where is he?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I don’t know.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought the man who had once been blind to the Pharisees.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now it was a Sabbath on the day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Pharisees also asked him again how he had gained his sight. He said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So some of the Pharisees said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Others said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can a person who is a sinner perform such signs?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there was a division among them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to the blind man again,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you say about him, since it was your eyes he opened?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He is a prophet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jewish leaders, then, did not believe that he had been blind and had gained his sight, until they summoned the parents of the man who had gained his sight

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and asked them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His parents answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: but how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders, for the Jewish leaders had already agreed that anyone who acknowledged him as Messiah would be put out of the synagogue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why his parents said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He is of age; ask him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So for a second time they summoned the man who had been blind and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I know: I was blind, and now I see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Surely you don’t want to become his disciples too?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They hurled abuse at him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are that man’s disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why, this is the astonishing thing: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is devout and does his will, God listens to that person.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Never since time began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a person born blind.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You were born wholly in sins, and you are teaching us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they threw him out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and when he found him he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “And who is he, sir, so that I may believe in him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You have seen him; in fact, he is the one speaking with you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I believe, Lord,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he bowed down before him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Surely we are not blind too?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If you were blind, you would have no sin. But now you say, ‘We see.’ Your sin remains.”

notes.traditional: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him
notes.note: The Greek has only ‘but so that’, with no verb; ‘it was’ is supplied, as in most translations, making the blindness serve God’s purpose. Some interpreters instead read the clause as describing an outcome, not a purpose. Others attach it to the next sentence: ‘But so that the works of God may be displayed in him, we must work…’. The ancient manuscripts had no punctuation to settle the matter.

The earliest manuscripts read ‘we must work’, drawing the disciples into Jesus’s task; many later manuscripts read ‘I must work’, which is the form familiar from the King James Version. ‘We’ is generally judged original, since copyists would more readily smooth it to match ‘the one who sent me’ than the reverse.

Siloam was a pool at the southern end of Jerusalem, fed by a channel from the Gihon spring. John connects its name with the Hebrew verb ‘to send’; in this Gospel Jesus is repeatedly called the one whom the Father sent, as in verse 4, so the gloss is probably meant to be heard as more than a geographical aside.

The Greek is simply ‘I am’ (egō eimi), the ordinary way of saying ‘It’s me’. They are the same two words Jesus uses in the weightier statement at 8:58, but here they are plain self-identification by the healed man.

The narrator mentions the mud deliberately. Kneading is listed among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath in later rabbinic tradition, and treating a condition that was not life-threatening on the Sabbath was also disputed. This explains the charge in verse 16 that Jesus does not keep the Sabbath.

The Greek word is ‘the Jews’, but everyone in this story is Jewish: the man, his parents, the neighbors and Jesus. The group meant here is the authorities who conduct the inquiry and can impose penalties (verse 22), apparently the same people called Pharisees in verses 13–16. Scholars are divided on how best to render the term in John; some prefer ‘Judeans’, others keep ‘the Jews’ throughout.

The Greek christos is here a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and not a name; the question is whether Jesus is that figure. ‘Messiah’ conveys the title to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

The Greek is a single adjective, found only in John (here, 12:42 and 16:2), meaning ‘excluded from the synagogue’, that is, cut off from the local Jewish community and its common life. Many scholars think the verse reflects conflicts between synagogues and Jesus’s followers in the decades after his death; others hold that local, informal exclusion was possible in his lifetime. The question is disputed.

This is not an invitation to thank God for the healing. It is a solemn formula charging a person to tell the truth or own up, as when Joshua says the same to Achan in Joshua 7:19. The interrogators are demanding that the man admit Jesus is a sinner.

The earliest manuscripts read ‘Son of Man’; most later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘Son of God’. ‘Son of Man’ is almost certainly original, since copyists would naturally replace it with the more usual object of belief and are unlikely to have done the opposite.

The same Greek address, kyrie, appears in verses 36 and 38. It ranges from a polite ‘sir’ to ‘Lord’ as a confession. In verse 36 the man does not yet know who the Son of Man is, so ‘sir’ fits; in verse 38, after Jesus identifies himself and the man declares his belief, ‘Lord’ is used. The shift is an interpretive choice that English forces and the Greek does not mark.

The Greek verb denotes the physical act of prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king or another person of high rank; the English ‘worship’ has narrowed to religious devotion alone. Most translations have ‘worshiped’, and many interpreters think John intends that full sense here, following the man’s confession. A few early manuscripts lack verse 38 and the opening words of verse 39, though most scholars regard them as original.

candidates.reason: Occurs across the Gospels, Acts and Revelation with objects ranging from God to human superiors; the choice between ‘worship’ and ‘bow down’ carries Christological weight and should be decided once.
Frequent in John and Paul; translators vary between reveal, manifest, show, display and make known, and it needs to be kept distinct from ἀποκαλύπτω.
Central to John and common in the Synoptics and Acts; translations waver between ‘sign’ and ‘miracle’, which obscures John’s deliberate use of the word.
The vocative κύριε addressed to Jesus recurs throughout the Gospels and a rule is needed for when it is ‘sir’ and when ‘Lord’, since the choice signals the speaker’s level of recognition.
Occurs only three times, all in John (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), and should be rendered identically in each so readers can see the thread.
